title: Discussions of Asperger Syndrome on Social Media: Content and Sentiment Analysis on Twitter
screen_reason: Cross-sectional content analysis of 227 popular English tweets (>30 likes) containing 'Aspergers' or 'Aspie', posted 1 May - 14 May 2021. Two autism-expert coders classified every tweet as providing correct information, containing misinformation, or neutral, giving a share of items in a sample coded as misinformation (4/227 = 1.8%) — a CONTENT prevalence with an explicit denominator.

estimates.country: Not stated (English-language tweets, no country restriction)
estimates.date: May 1 to May 14, 2021 (the week before and the week after Musk's 8 May 2021 disclosure)
estimates.measure_type: % of popular Asperger-related tweets classified by two expert coders as containing misinformation
estimates.value_raw: 4 (1.8%) of the 227 tweets classified as containing misinformation
estimates.denominator: 227 popular original tweets (>30 likes) in English containing the terms "Aspergers" or "Aspie", retrieved with Twitter advanced search for 1-14 May 2021 (34 before and 193 after Musk's disclosure)
estimates.definition: Post classified by 2 independent autism-expert coders as containing misinformation rather than correct or neutral information; the coding example given is "people with Asperger have an IQ below average"; identified misinformative tweets included claims that autism and Asperger result from asymmetrical brain stem injuries
estimates.misinfo_def: "Each post was classified by 2 independent coders who are experts in autism (IS and ANH) as to whether the post contained correct information (eg, 'people with Asperger have difficulties in social interaction'), misinformation (eg, 'people with Asperger have an IQ below average'), or neutral information (eg, 'my son has Asperger')."
estimates.source_quote: We classified 210 (92.5%) of the 227 tweets as being neutral, 13 (5.7%) tweets as informative, and 4 (1.8%) as containing misinformation.
estimates.page_loc: Results, 'Informative, Neutral, and Misinformative Tweets Following Musk's Announcement' (also in the Abstract)
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two independent coders who are experts in autism (authors IS and ANH) applied a written coding guideline deposited in the study's Zenodo repository; disagreements resolved by discussion with the remaining coauthors until consensus. Interrater agreement kappa = 0.469, described by the authors as moderate.
estimates.moderator_quote: We used the Twitter advanced search engine to find popular tweets (>30 likes) that were posted in English and included the terms "Aspergers" or "Aspie." ... We defined popular tweets as those with more than 30 likes as this is slightly higher than the average of 25 likes reported in previous research.
estimates.notes: CONTENT rather than QUALITY: tweets were judged true/false against expert knowledge of Asperger syndrome with an explicit misinformation category, not scored on a quality instrument. denom_selection = curated because the sample is truncated by popularity (>30 likes), not a random or full sample of Asperger tweets; sampling_frame = keyword_topical (two search terms, single issue). confidence = medium because kappa = 0.469 is only moderate and the numerator is 4 items, so the estimate is very imprecise; the authors also note they cannot rule out bot accounts. No country is reported; only English-language tweets were collected.

missed_or_uncertain: 1) Before/after split not extracted as separate rows: the paper says 34 tweets were posted before and 193 after the disclosure and that 'Both informative and misinformative tweets were posted after Musk's disclosure', which would imply 0/34 before and 4/193 (2.1%) after. Neither share is stated verbatim and the 'after' one depends on reading the sentence as meaning all four, so under R8 I kept only the pooled 1.8%. 2) The 13 (5.7%) informative and 210 (92.5%) neutral shares are the complements of the misinformation share and are not misinformation prevalence, so no rows. 3) Engagement means (comments, retweets, likes) for the 4 misinformative tweets in Table 1 are per-post means, not a share of engagement, so no SHARING or CONCENTRATION row is possible; the paper reports no share of retweets or likes that carried misinformation. 4) Sentiment (AFINN) scores are not a falsity measure.

rob.design: Cross-sectional content analysis of a popularity-truncated keyword sample: Twitter advanced search for English original tweets with >30 likes containing 'Aspergers' or 'Aspie', 1-14 May 2021, n = 227 (34 before / 193 after Musk's 8 May disclosure). Two independent autism-expert coders classified each post as correct information, misinformation, or neutral using a deposited coding guideline; disagreements resolved by consensus with coauthors; interrater agreement kappa = 0.469 (moderate). Sentiment scored with AFINN; analyses in SPSS 25; data and scripts deposited on Zenodo. No response-rate concept (platform data). Authors' stated limits: one two-week window, English only, >30-likes threshold, Twitter users unrepresentative of the population, possible bot accounts, no user-level data.
